reverse_outline.summary: Three-bullet preview: sensible team choices produce an unplanned landscape, the fix is to decide and unburden once, and five parts make up the model
Corvane's teams ended up with four deploy methods, three brokers and two identity libraries that nobody chose as a whole
Decree and laissez-faire both skip the question of which decisions to make once, because the cost of variety shows only across teams
Part IV's claim that settling decisions once and removing shared load once keeps engineering changeable, spelled out as five things / roadmap of this page and the five chapter questions
Two repeated costs, divergent decisions and rebuilt mechanics, each with one remedy: a policy and a platform
Two limits on the remedies, judgment by the teams served and enforcement proportional to divergence cost, mapped to the book's product-thinking and system-design lenses

results.quote: The limit on enforcement is system design: it says where a decision sits, with a team or with the whole organization.
results.finding: Flow reader B (a): the limits are introduced as judging first, enforcement second, then matched to the lenses in the opposite order, and B could not see how 'enforced no harder than the cost of divergence warrants' says where a decision sits; stayed unsure. Flow reader A noted the reversed order too but rated it (b), so the point is not rated (a) by both and is recorded as minor.

results.quote: Both remedies have limits. A policy and a platform exist for the teams that deliver to users, so they are judged by those teams
results.finding: Both flow readers rated (b): being judged by the teams reads as a criterion, not a limit, and the start of the second limit ('And a rule is enforced...') is not marked; resolved on reaching 'The two limits'. Minor.

results.draft_locus: Five Parts of One Engineering Model ¶1
results.quote: the fourth keeps what was decided in force in daily work
results.finding: Flow reader A only (a): the quality bullet says nothing about policies or decisions, so the reader went back from the bullet to the grouping sentence and stayed unsure how quality 'keeps decisions in force'; only 'the teams' quality practices use them every day' in the next paragraph half-explains it. Not reported by reader B; minor.

results.quote: Once a platform team is justified, which [[team-types]] in Part II decides, how is the platform funded, run and judged as a product, and what does developer experience measure?
results.finding: Both flow readers rated (b): 'which [[team-types]] in Part II decides' is first read as a question about which team type decides and has to be re-parsed as a relative clause. The AC-1 cold reader carried the misreading into the answer ('once a platform team is justified, who decides'). Reader B also needed a second read of the same nested clause in Introduction ¶3. Resolved by re-reading, so minor.

Every does_not_know term the draft uses is glossed where it is defined: message broker and identity library (¶1), policy and platform (Decide Once ¶1), diagnosis, advice, decision record, nudge, paved path, guardrail, tax, mandate, developer experience, specialists versus a gate, technical debt and migration (the list); stream-aligned team is recalled from Part II. 'Policies' and the governance terms appear in the lead before their gloss but are flagged 'each defined below'. The three phases of a migration are not named, and the draft does not use the term. Reader B's (b) note on 'shared load' is covered by ¶2's 'mechanics of deploying built and maintained four times over' and the next section's opening question.
Opens on a concrete scenario and a question; no dictionary definition, apology, announcement-only or sweeping-generality opening.
The closing adds a synthesis (the life of a decision) and a hand-off; it does not merely restate, apologize or raise an unrelated new point.

Synthesis ('follow a technical decision through its life: where it is made ... how it is changed') and so-what ('a leader spends effort on the decisions that recur ... takes off product teams') are both present, with the takeaway and the hand-off to engineering-strategy.

'At Corvane nobody had asked which of its choices should be made once, so each team answered for itself, which is why every choice could be reasonable and the sum could not' reads the opening landscape against the lead's question, as the spec's callback states.
The cold intro reader predicted both roadmap promises in order: the two repeated costs with a remedy each, then the five parts of the model, closing on five chapters answering five questions.

The cold reader named the five subjects in reading order: engineering strategy; architecture governance; platforms and developer experience; quality and reliability; migrations and technical debt. (The reader's 'who decides' under chapter 15 is the misparse recorded under flow_is_followable; the subject and order are right.)
